answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) resources are under the Microsoft.DocumentDB provider. The account resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example to create a MongoDB-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. For Mongo DB-specific child resources use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and .../mongodbCollections. Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" for the account and resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database" / "azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection" for DBs/collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use the MongoDB driver connection string. Typical form: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin. (You can also use mongodb+srv with a SRV record where supported.)

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units). You provision RU/s at account/database/container level or use autoscale (RU/s autoscale). Cosmos also offers serverless consumption mode in supported regions — compute is not exposed as vCore tiers for Cosmos DB's MongoDB API.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane access uses MongoDB-style username/password (SCRAM) credentials issued by the Cosmos account (primary/secondary keys or created Mongo users). There is not a direct MongoDB-driver-to-Entra authentication flow; if you want to use an Entra credential you must exchange an Azure identity for an ARM-managed key or use management APIs to obtain a key, then use that key as the MongoDB password. In short: use standard Mongo authentication; Azure AD/Entra identity is for management/RBAC, not direct Mongo auth in most Cosmos MongoDB API setups.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB client drivers for your language (e.g., npm package mongodb for Node.js). There is no separate data-plane, Mongo-specific SDK from Azure for application queries; the azure sdk (azure-cosmos) is for the Core (SQL) API and management only.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Expected vector index types used in Azure/Cosmos vector work are HNSW and IVF (and vendor-provided DiskANN in some builds). In a MongoDB-compatible API the create-index call is expressed with createIndex on the collection and an index-specifying options document. Example (synthetic): db.articles.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vec_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }). (Exact option names differ by service version; adapt to the cluster's index-creation API.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text search is typically performed by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (or the service's integrated search capability where available). Hybrid search (text + vector) is usually implemented by combining a vector index (for similarity) with text indexes/ranking in the search layer (Azure Cognitive Search or the cluster's vector+text index features). In practice you either push documents into Azure Cognitive Search (which supports hybrid ranking) or use the cluster's combined text+vector index if the cluster build provides that capability.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API implements a specific MongoDB wire protocol version and supports a subset of server features; historically supported server versions have included 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4 (and newer versions were added over time). Not all MongoDB server features are available: some aggregation stages, server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands, some transaction semantics across partitions, and some admin/system collections can be limited or unsupported. Verify the exact supported wire/server version for your account and adapt code to the supported feature set.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (Microsoft-provided emulator image). The emulator exposes the MongoDB-compatible endpoint on the same emulator host; when emulating Mongo API you typically connect to localhost with the Mongo port used by Cosmos (10255) and with TLS enabled. The emulator image is mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator (or the Windows installer).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change Streams are available on some supported MongoDB protocol versions of the Cosmos DB Mongo API. If available you can consume them like standard MongoDB change streams (watch()). There may be account-level or API-version requirements to enable the feature depending on the Cosmos release; check the account's supported features and API compatibility version before relying on them.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The service-specific MCP server is called documentdb (the 'documentdb' MCP server) — use that profile to access collection/index inspection and query-plan tooling. The general azure MCP server does not expose the service-specific Mongo/Cosmos debugging helpers, so use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane inspection.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft's original hosted JSON DB was called DocumentDB; it was rebranded/expanded into Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB exposes a 'DocumentDB' (SQL) API and also provides a MongoDB-compatible API. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is unrelated to other projects named DocumentDB (and is not the same as Amazon DocumentDB).

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The engine underneath is Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed document store that implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility. That means application code uses standard MongoDB drivers, but some MongoDB server features, semantics and edge-case behaviors can differ (indexing, transactions, aggregation stage support and limits). Test against the target account to ensure feature compatibility.

answers.question: Which database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_fintech_15 for all sample-created collections and data.

answers.question: What collection and vector index definition will this sample create for article embeddings?
answers.answer: Create a collection named articles in sample_fintech_15 and add a vector index on the embedding field. Example (pseudo-Mongo): db.getSiblingDB('sample_fintech_15').createCollection('articles'); db.articles.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embedding_vec_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }); (Adjust option names to the cluster's index-creation API.)

answers.question: How should the sample read the connection information at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI (process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI). Pass that URI to MongoClient.connect(uri, { tls: true, useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }) at application startup. Do not persist the raw value into fixtures or source control.

answers.question: Which Node.js client package and version should the sample install and use?
answers.answer: Install and use the official mongodb driver from npm (e.g., npm install mongodb). Target a recent 4.x/5.x driver version compatible with the cluster — use the MongoClient API (const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb')).

answers.question: Which host suffix and port will the sample expect in the connection string?
answers.answer: Expect the host to be <account-name>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com (or an SRV name) and the TLS MongoDB port 10255. Use a connection string like: mongodb://<user>:<pass>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin
